name: Abdul Samad Zeeshan
role: I build backend and data systems
intro: I finished my Computing Science degree at the University of Alberta in June 2026. I build backend services, data pipelines and systems with a language model. Each project below solves one real problem.

edges.evidence: I wrote the agent, its server and the risk score code in Python. A script rebuilds the result tables from saved files.
A LangGraph agent gathers the facts on each change, but it never has the power to approve anything alone.
The agent reaches its tools through a Model Context Protocol server. None of 84 attacks over that link succeeded.
The agent gets each tool only when a step needs it. It gets the power to write only after the risk score is ready.
Each credential is short-lived and names one customer and one request. The server answered no call from seven types of forged credential.
The same defences held when Warden used a real login server and a Postgres database. None of the 84 attacks succeeded there.
The approval rules are in one file with a version number. A solver compares each new version with the last one before use.
A test fails if a result table in the write-up differs from the saved result files.
I wrote the made-up customers, the recorder between agent and tools, and the report in Python, with automated tests.
It tests an AI agent on made-up customers. The agent's tools are recordings or fakes, so the agent cannot change anything real.
Hostile made-up customers pushed the old Warden into about 1.3 unwanted server calls per conversation. The new version made 0.6, so it shipped.
I tuned three automatic judges on known answers. Then I checked them against the true outcome of 240 sample calls.
A run recorded with a local model replays in automated tests with no model at all.
The service is plain Java on the built-in web server, with lightweight threads and hand-written JSON.
Database rules support the ledger rules. Each payment key is unique, ordinary balances cannot go below zero, and no entry is zero.
Tally applies a retried payment only once, even after a lost reply. It applied none of about 1,600 retries twice.
Tally locks account rows in one fixed order, so two transfers that cross can never block each other forever.
A TLA+ model follows the transfer code line by line. A proof tool checked about 390,000 different situations and found no error.
I made the network and database fail while transfers continued. In about 11,000 transfers, Tally did not lose or double one cent.
I deploy Tally to a local Kubernetes cluster from plain config files. Each release must pass four checks and a failure test.
On new data, 82% of the transfers that Tally flagged were fraud. This is up from 37% with the first rules.
A checker rebuilt 16 fraud signals for all 9,290 payments with only earlier data. It found no mismatches.
I wrote the metrics by hand. Each speed figure starts when the request was due to leave, so time in the queue counts.
A small, fixed web API gives access to the ledger, with no framework.
Automated checks rerun the failure tests on every push as the fifth release check.
I wrote the conversation logic, the booking service and the tests in Python. The tests need no models.
Speech recognition works offline on one laptop. Only 17 of 40 test calls ended in a booking. That is not good enough yet.
When the booking system failed during a call, Parley handled it safely all 232 times. It never spoke a false fact.
I replay the same scripted calls with clean audio, noisy audio, damaged text and a broken booking system.
Tests make the booking system slow, empty, inconsistent or unavailable during a call. Parley then books a callback and does not guess.
Automated checks fail if the tables in the write-up differ from the result file.
I wrote the detector, the checker and the score code in Python. They read a local copy of the full login log.
Batch scores and live scores use the same Spark code on the full log of about a billion events.
The first version keeps a dbt and DuckDB warehouse over the stored logins.
Tarn scores each login when it arrives. Logins in the same second never see each other.
The first version keeps a Neo4j graph of which user logged into which computer.
I recalculated about 5.1 million detector inputs with all later data hidden. None changed, so no input used future data.
With 100 alerts a day, Tarn caught the attacker on 29 of 181 days. The first rules caught 21. It still missed most days.
Every detector learns only from the first day. I score each one against the lab's answer key and keep the bad results.
An AI analyst asks questions about the login map through a fixed list of tools. Tarn refuses any made-up tool call.
The analyst's confidence was near its true hit rate, off by 0.04 with map tools and 0.05 without. The sample was only 49 alerts.
Automated checks run the same code on a small saved part of the log. They fail if the tables change.
I wrote the code that trains and scores the model in Python.
After fine-tuning, the small model gave the right urgency to 87% of new support emails. Before training, it got 38% right.
A large hosted model labels the emails, and the small model learns to copy those labels.
It returns topic, urgency and account number as clean JSON, offline, with no outside service.
It put 90% of the same 1,200 emails in the right topic. Before training, it got 64% right.
I wrote the pipeline, its tests and its score code in TypeScript.
Docket uses AWS storage, queues, functions and a database. I deployed it to a test account, checked it, then removed it.
With a forced output format, the model read all 20 photo receipts into valid JSON. Without it, 17 of 20 were valid.
Claude Haiku on Amazon Bedrock got almost every field right on 42 receipts that I checked by hand. It used saved answers.
With a 1% error budget, Docket let 11 of 149 test receipts skip a person. None of their 32 fields was wrong.
Each record's id comes from the file itself, so a repeated delivery never makes a second record.
The alarms stopped because a security setting removed their right to publish, with no warning. The alarm topic now grants it in writing.
I wrote a second copy of the exchange in Python. Random tests check that both copies give the same answer.
One thread owns the order book, and queues pass orders in and out. Four replays of 5 million orders gave the same bytes.
A TLA+ model checked about 540,000 situations of the exchange and found no broken rule. It caught both bugs I added on purpose.
I tune each trading robot on earlier days and test it once on the next day. None of the honest robots made money.
